title: sufr reads its input through libsail's Reader and FastaParser
body:
`read_sequence_file` in `libsufr/src/build.rs` reads the input with needletail's `parse_fastx_file`. For each record it pushes the delimiter, records where the record starts, and copies `rec.seq()` into the text. It takes the record's name as the id up to its first whitespace. `normalize` then makes one more pass over the whole text. It maps every byte through a table for soft masking and records which bytes occur.

sufr-409cc8 asks whether `libsail` reads the input faster than needletail. This issue says how sufr would read through `libsail` if the answer is yes.

## Proposal

Frame each record with `libsail::index::Reader` and parse it with `libsail::seq::fasta::FastaParser::parse`, then copy the record's `seq` into the text.

- `Reader::new(file, Format::Fasta)` frames one record at a time out of a stream. `advance()` moves to the next record. `record()` returns that record's bytes, header line included.
- `FastaParser::parse(record)` returns a `FastaRecord`. Its `name` is the header up to the first whitespace, and its `seq` holds the residues with all ASCII whitespace dropped.

```rust
let mut reader = Reader::new(File::open(path)?, Format::Fasta);
while reader.advance()? {
    let record = FastaParser::parse(reader.record())?;
    text.extend_from_slice(&record.seq);
}
```

sufr keeps its fallback name for a record whose header has no name.

## Measurements

sail-ce02ff timed this loop against needletail on 1 GiB inputs. With the changes noted there, on an AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D:

| input | needletail | `Reader` and `parse` |
|---|---|---|
| DNA, wrapped at 60 | 0.373 s | 0.367 s |
| DNA, one line per record | 0.137 s | 0.261 s |
| protein | 0.492 s | 0.433 s |

needletail is ahead on one-line records because it borrows such a record's sequence from its buffer and never copies it. sail-ce02ff is still working on that row.

## Rejected

- Copying the residues in sufr with a per-byte filter on `is_ascii_whitespace`. sail-ce02ff measured that loop at the speed of the old `parse`, two to four times slower than needletail.
- A `libsail` function that appends a record's residues to a buffer the caller owns. sail-56ab6e proposed it and was dropped. sufr was its only caller.

## Cost

- `libsail` reads neither FASTQ nor gzip, and needletail reads both today. `Reader::new` takes any `Read`, so sufr could hand it a gzip decoder. `libsail` has no FASTQ reader.
- `Reader` holds the current record whole in its buffer. Peak memory grows by the largest record, which in hg38 is a chromosome.

## Open

- Whether sufr can drop FASTQ input, or keeps needletail for it.
